articles.title_orig: Record diesel prices drive UK inflation to 1-year high of 3.6%
articles.title_zh: Record diesel prices drive UK inflation to 1-year high of 3.6%
articles.content_orig:
U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, its highest level in a year, as fuel costs continued to rise.
The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.
October's reading puts U.K. inflation at a one-year high.
Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated.
The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September.
Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Bank of England's final meeting of the year.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the release that a recent climb down in oil prices following the U.S. midterm elections could offer some relief in future inflation readings.
But he added: "While this may be a short-term reprieve for motorists, the broader outlook for UK inflation remains challenging as we approach 2027. After hiking interest rates at the start of the month, the Bank will be wary of a sustained uptick in inflation that could be here to stay."

articles.title_orig: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.title_zh: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping opened a key Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting on Wednesday with calls for removing trade and investment barriers.
The leader spoke as he was expected to host Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump this week alongside the APEC CEO and Economic Leaders Summit.
"We should remove trade and investment barriers," Xi said via an official English translation. He said a key reason for doing so was "to promote development that is balanced."
He did not mention U.S. tariffs or other specific measures. Instead, Xi cast China as a "promising land for development" for global businesses, and indicated plans for "Bay Area" cooperation.
Shenzhen, home to major Chinese tech companies, is part of China's "Greater Bay Area" that includes Hong Kong and Macau. The Silicon Valley region around San Francisco is also known as the "Bay Area" in the U.S.
"China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further," Xi said. He said China would "reform" rules and regulations to give foreign businesses "full manufacturing access."
Chinese exports have steadily grown their share of global manufactured goods, drawing criticism from the European Union and other regions for overcapacity. The U.S. and China last year agreed to keep tariffs lower, but the world's two largest economies have yet to implement a planned $30 billion cut in duties on goods from each side.
"Global growth lacks momentum," Xi noted in his speech. But he said "still global trade keeps growing against headwinds, and breakthroughs are being made in emerging technologies at a faster pace."
He said the "hard questions of our times" for Asia Pacific economies is whether to open, or close, doors — and later cast opening doors as bringing "progress."
"There can be no stability without security, and no security without stability," he said.
Xi called for APEC members to deepen coordination in the digital economy and AI, as a way to drive regional economic growth.
"Unicorn companies and large AI models have emerged in large numbers and many innovations have empowered hundreds of trades and industries and reached millions of households," he said, in some of his most specific mentions of the cutting-edge technology.

articles.title_orig: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.title_zh: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_zh: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.title_zh: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.content_orig:
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

articles.title_zh: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, a ministry spokesperson said in response to a media query.

Guided by the important consensus reached between the leaders of the two countries, China and Canada have held multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations in the spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation, reaching a supplementary joint arrangement on trade issues of mutual concern, the spokesperson said.
The two sides also reached positive consensus on economic and trade issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment, according to the spokesperson.
READ MORE: Commerce ministry: China willing to lengthen cooperation list with Canada
The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Both sides will expedite their respective domestic procedures to put the agreed measures into effect as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the two countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations.
The preliminary joint arrangement between China and Canada was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."

Xiaomi took the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max global at an event in Paris today , and it seems like the vanilla Xiaomi 18 wants a bit of the spotlight too. A tipster on X has shared what's purportedly the first live image of the phone, which you can see below.
The white unit in the photo has a metal frame and a squircle camera island with three cameras. Unlike its Pro siblings, however, there's no secondary display on the back.
The tipster also shared the phone's expected specs, which mostly (but not entirely) line up with what leaked back in September . The Xiaomi 18 is said to have a flat 6.4-inch "1.5K" 120Hz LTPO OLED with TCL's M11 panel, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, a 200MP main camera with OIS, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 50MP telephoto with OIS, along with a battery of around 7,000 mAh with 100W wired charging. It's also tipped to come with an IP69 rating, an ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, and a USB 3.2 port.
That telephoto is a bit of a departure from the September leak, which claimed the Xiaomi 18 would get a 200MP periscope with 3x optical zoom, just like the Pro models. The battery was also tipped at 7,200 mAh back then. The phone is expected to launch in China in December, so we should know for sure soon enough.

articles.title_orig: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.title_zh: Fed official Lisa Cook refuses to attend White House firing hearing, citing bias
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.content_orig:
AI investors and beyond were eagerly anticipating Nvidia's ( NVDA -0.44% ) earnings call Tuesday night. The earnings report was the company's first since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid controversy last week. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO as it conducts a search for a permanent replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
Kress passed her first test with flying colors, as she delivered a confident pitch for the company and even raised guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% revenue growth to 75% revenue growth. Nvidia also beat estimates on the top and bottom lines, and the stock was trading higher after the call, up 3.3% as of 8:23 p.m.
However, amid the focus on the headline numbers and parsing the call for hints into the company's future, there was one key comment from Kress that investors may have missed.
It's understandable why Nvidia is down a third from its peak last month, given Huang's sudden exit, but with Nvidia stock now trading at a forward P/E of just 11, the stock is as cheap as it's ever been and ripe for share buybacks.
In response to a question about the company's capital allocation and its buyback plans, Kress said that the "super top priority" for returning capital to shareholders was to use the company's current share repurchase authorization, which was raised by $150 billion in September and sat at $227.3 billion at the end of the third quarter. Kress added, "So thinking about all of that together, I think there is definitely room to continue all of the stock repurchase plans that we want to do and complete those before the end of fiscal year '28." She also noted that the top priority for its capital spending is supporting its suppliers in building out additional capacity.
If Nvidia executes on those buybacks and the stock price stays roughly the same, it would reduce shares outstanding by roughly 6% by Jan. 2028, when fiscal 2028 ends.
The share repurchase authorization and Kress's commitment are a positive sign, not just because it will lift Nvidia's earnings per share, but because it shows management's confidence that the stock is undervalued after the recent sell-off and signals to investors that it's worth buying.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/17/26
For investors worried that Nvidia would struggle during the transitional period, Kress gave no indication that anything has changed, saying, "it's business as usual," and that customers, suppliers, and partners are all "100% behind us."
Demand for the company's products continues to outstrip supply, and Kress spent much of the call reiterating the company's commitment to securing adequate supply, which allowed it to raise its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028.
In just one quarter, its supply commitments increased from $279 billion, primarily due to memory supply. Kress said, "We feel confident in terms of both the demand that we have in front of us as well as the supply and additionally that we can do the 75%," referring to 75% revenue growth next year.
Nvidia also addressed the controversy around Jensen Huang, and new Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones made it clear that the board has no intention of reinstating Huang. Regarding the CEO search, Jones said, "We want to install this CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, who has been seen as a possible replacement for Huang, was on the Q&A portion of the call, but did not answer any questions.
Nvidia did what it needed to do on the earnings call and then some. Its commitment to using up its $227 billion share repurchase authorization and the guidance hike for fiscal 2028 show investors the company continues to excel. Nvidia is on track to bring in more than $700 billion in revenue next year. Given the deep discount, Nvidia looks like a buy , even without Jensen Huang.

articles.title_orig: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.title_zh: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.content_orig:
Chief Correspondent covering media and technology
Did AI cause the US government to shut down all air travel Friday?
Could be, says the US government.
Also, maybe not. Who knows? But don't worry.
That's the confusing answer from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He went on Fox News on Monday and said that the nationwide grounding last week — as well as other recent high-profile outages at places like JPMorgan, Microsoft , and United — might have all stemmed from organizations introducing new AI software into their IT stacks.
Why does he think that? Because "one guy that's very smart with tech," — not Elon Musk, Mullin specified — told him that. And "that kinda makes sense to me."
I mean, it also kinda makes sense to me? Maybe? But I'm not running a federal agency with more than 200,000 workers and an annual budget of more than $100 billion.
But Mullin said he really doesn't know. He does know that "we just have a lot of technologists [sic] thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems. And the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."
Then Mullin told Fox viewers that they should "breathe." And be assured that the US is probably not under a cyber attack — something he felt "98%" confident about.
I would very much like to live in a world where a top federal official doesn't muddle through national news interviews about outages. I would very much like to live in a world where the administration hadn't spent much of last year telling us the federal government was incompetent and should be radically downsized . Because sometimes we really want the federal government — not "one guy" — to be able to tell us what's actually happening inside these complicated systems, and what should be done about it.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
But I also think we'd have these exact same problems if we had the most competent, well-meaning public servants in charge right now.
That's because all of this stuff is gnarly and complicated. Long before the AI boom, we've had technologists pointing out how rickety and poorly maintained much of America's digital and physical infrastructure is — and how seemingly isolated problems can have enormous ripple effects. Perhaps you recall the giant blackout of 2003 , where big swaths of the country, including New York City, lost power because of a software glitch in Ohio.
Now we've added AI to the mix —a technology so new and head-scratching that the people who are building it frequently say they're not really sure how it works , and aren't exactly sure how to control it .
Which is why people who have talked to more than "one guy" often tell us to buckle up for more instability. "We should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time," as journalist Josh Tyrangiel put it in The Atlantic .
What can you, a normal person, do about this? Here I agree with Markwayne Mullin: You shouldn't do anything. There's nothing much you can do, aside from the digital equivalent of making sure you have some soup cans and water bottles handy, just in case.
But if you're a member of the media — that is, anyone with access to a keyboard and an internet connection — things get a little trickier. It is reasonable to cover all of these outages, ask why they're happening, and not accept the hand-wavy answers you often get right after an event. But also be ready to accept that sometimes things break because things break, and that sometimes a coincidence is a coincidence. Or that maybe it's all a squirrel's fault .
That's not an easy balance to pull off. Ring the bell every time there's a possible threat, and you'll end up with a country that's permanently on edge — or worse, doesn't pay attention to any warnings at all. Wait too long before ringing the bell, and people may be woefully unprepared. It's a real challenge .
That said, one very easy step is to just stay mute when you don't have anything helpful to say.
Tuesday morning, I got asked to come on an interview show to discuss "the November 17 blackout," which confused me since I was unaware there had been a blackout Tuesday.
Turns out it was a reference to a made-up thing on social media , and I'm not going to spend more time discussing a non-thing here.
Except to say that it's one thing for your uncle to pass along a hoax email to his friends and family. And it's another to go on TV or the internet and give the hoax that much more oxygen. Even if you're ostensibly going to debunk the hoax, you're still spreading the particulates around.
But Markwayne Mullin? I'd definitely like you to ask a few more people — perhaps there are still technology experts in your organization, for starters — for more information. Then come back and tell us what you've learned. We'd love to know more.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft calls Copilot "the new OS for work" at Ignite keynote
articles.title_zh: Microsoft calls Copilot "the new OS for work" at Ignite keynote
articles.content_orig:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.”
The announcement is a striking inversion of how we’ve traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent’s work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.
The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign the company first announced in September. Parts of that vision are now becoming “generally available,” as Nadella puts it, with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside them.
Copilot Autopilot (not to be confused with Windows Autopilot) is a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” according to Microsoft. In a nutshell, Autopilot is a cloud-based autonomous AI agent that users can delegate responsibilities to, not just single tasks. Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete tasks assigned to it as part of its role. Autopilot will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, but final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.
Also announced as generally available at the keynote speech was Microsoft IQ , an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ , a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies want autonomous agents to have access to internal documents and messaging data will have to be determined by their own internal IT review.
Copilot Workspaces is a collaborative environment currently available through Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, but coming soon will be the ability to bring personal Autopilot agents into Workspaces. Early in the keynote address, Nadella said that “Until now, AI interactions have mostly been single-player. Workspaces makes it a truly multiplayer experience, where people and agents drive towards a common goal, with shared context.”
Trust, the third pillar of Microsoft’s new frontier ecosystem, was something that Nadella continued returning to during his presentation, and not in a way that some might expect. “We find ourselves in a place where alignment is elusive. Mechanistic understanding of these models is elusive. The question is: How can you even trust all this powerful technology? The reality is, by definition, you can’t,” he said.
In a departure from the norms of “AI is magic” corporate hype sentiment, Nadella conceded that the internal workings of AI thought processes remain difficult to understand, and models cannot be trusted to govern themselves, regardless of whether their answers are accurate. Nadella described the solution as “an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence” from the authority granted to it. Microsoft says each Autopilot agent will have a unique ID, and administrators can restrict permissions or block it entirely. All agent activities are logged for human review, and Autopilot can ask for human approval before engaging in certain actions.
The promised agent controls and admission that AI systems can’t always be trusted are meaningful, but Microsoft is asking businesses and users to place their trust in the company’s own safeguards instead, though the effectiveness of those safeguards against mistakes, rogue actions, or data exposure will still have to be demonstrated. In Microsoft’s view, the solution to untrustworthy intelligence is not to make AI agents trustworthy, but to control what they’re permitted to do. Businesses will have to decide how much autonomy they delegate to agents.
Along with the guardrails, Microsoft announced what it calls the “ AI Transparency Initiative .” The effort has partnered with 40-plus major companies, including Adobe and Mastercard, to develop open, industrywide standards for AI governance and security. Nadella described the initiative as a way for industry to “help establish an open standard that makes AI safer, more transparent, and more accessible.”
Along with the other announced additions, Microsoft also announced expanding capabilities for Agent 365 , its existing control plane for managing AI agents across enterprise environments. The new agent sheriff extends existing identity, security, and management systems to AI agents. Microsoft describes the objective as providing “observability at every layer of the stack.” Agent 365 offers governance controls over agent behavior in what Microsoft says is “autonomous in execution, but bounded and supervised.”
Along with Agent 365 comes Agent 365 Business Analytics : “You can simply think of this as an ERP system of AI usage. You can see exactly what’s driving the spend and connect the spend to the outcomes that drive business value,” said Nadella. Customers will be able to see real-world costs associated with AI token-spend, and compare those metrics to the value of work performed. Microsoft acknowledged that the estimations of assisted work hours are determined by a model , and not a direct measurement of time that may have been saved. This is a telling concession for Microsoft to make as businesses evaluate whether there will be an ROI on AI implementations, but according to Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial Business, “anything you can do with Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, for less .”
Nadella offered only a brief acknowledgment of last week’s outage that disrupted access to services like Exchange Online and Teams for users across the globe. “Last week was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world,” he said. “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously, and in that context I know we have work to do.”
That statement was all the time the elephant in the room was given, but Microsoft did seem to acknowledge the public’s growing concern over data center projects by highlighting the previously discussed “ community-first AI infrastructure plan .” Not a surprise in a presentation that asks organizations to extend more autonomy to software agents, at a time when Microsoft’s existing infrastructure is under increased scrutiny.

articles.title_orig: California DMV boots Waymo robotaxis off state freeways after string of incidents
articles.title_zh: California DMV boots Waymo robotaxis off state freeways after string of incidents
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Motor Vehicles has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after images showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
VIDEO: Driverless Waymo tries to bypass CHP traffic break on SF freeway
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told ABC7 Eyewitness News.
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026 , Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says these new restrictions went into effect on November 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
MORE: Study finds lower crash rate for Waymo vehicles in San Francisco
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. ABC7 Eyewitness News previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again Monday.
"I used to use it all the time and now it's like ehh I'll walk, or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

Marine Le Pen has pledged to tear up Emmanuel Macron’ s flagship pension overhaul and allow French workers who started their careers young to retire at 60 if she wins the 2027 presidential election.
Unveiling her economic programme on Tuesday, the National Rally front-runner sought to convince sceptical bond markets that she can deliver one of her party’s core promises to working-class voters without worsening France’s already-strained public finances.
At the centre of her proposal is a new €900bn (£750bn) retirement fund built up over a generation alongside France’s existing pay-as-you-go system, financed by redirecting a portion of existing employer payroll contributions.
“We are going to bring down one of the last privileges in our country, the privilege of access to the financial services that make a minority wealthy today, while also improving the financing of our national economy,” Ms Le Pen told reporters.
The far-right leader promised that hundreds of thousands of people would be able to leave work two to three years earlier than under Mr Macron’s legislation, which gradually lifts the minimum retirement age from 62 to 64.
France’s current statutory retirement age of 62 years and nine months is already well below the 65-to-67 benchmark across most major economies, even as French life expectancy ranks among the highest.
“For those who wonder whether the French social model will still be standing when they retire, I have heard them,” she said. “This reform is a promise for the future and an act of faith in the French model.”
“Hundreds of thousands of workers will retire earlier, gaining two to three years compared with what [Mr Macron’s] reform would have imposed,” she added.
President Macron’s 2023 pension changes provoked months of mass strikes and street protests before the government agreed to freeze their implementation in exchange for Socialist support on the budget.
But the higher retirement age threshold remains due to come into force in January 2028, shortly after the next president takes office.
How to fund France’s generous retirement system – the single biggest drain on the public purse, projected to cost more than €430bn (£360bn) next year – has become a central test for the National Rally’s economic credibility.
Ms Le Pen has committed to finding €138bn (£115bn) in wider public spending reductions by 2032, arguing that her overhaul would eventually generate up to €20bn (£17bn) in annual savings.
Economists and market analysts remain unconvinced that those figures add up if Mr Macron’s age increase is reversed.
To keep costs in check, National Rally is shifting emphasis away from a fixed age threshold towards the total number of years paid into the system.
Workers who entered employment early would qualify for retirement between 60 and 62 after 40 to 42 years of contributions, while university graduates would generally need to remain in work well into their sixties to receive a full pension.

Nvidia’s board has made clear that it will not bring Jensen Huang back as CEO after shareholders and his fellow tech bros called for him to be reinstated .
Huang resigned as head of the AI chipmaking company after he admitted to an affair with a Chinese executive suspected of being a spy for Beijing.
“Jensen Huang, voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia’s board, said during an earnings call Tuesday. Executives refused to take questions from investors about the scandal.
Nvidia’s better-than-expected third-quarter earnings report caused its stock to pop in after-hours trading. Nvidia’s stock sat at $155.46 at the closing bell, and just thirty minutes later, it spiked by about 4 percent to $161.69.
The company reported revenues of $115.8 billion, beating Wall Street’s estimates of around $109 billion.
On November 8, the day Huang admitted the affair to employees, Nvidia said it would be conducting an investigation following reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang stepped down last Thursday and was replaced by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, while the company looks for a permanent CEO.
Over the weekend, an online petition to reinstate Huang as Nvidia’s CEO garnered more than 100,000 signatures , including around 60,000 from shareholders, 6,000 from current Nvidia employees and 1,000 from former employees, according to reports.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney publicly backed the effort, and there was a report that Huang had discussions with allies about possibly returning to the helm .
One ally told the Financial Times that they were convening a “war room” of tech executives to reinstate Huang and would try to get support from the White House.
President Donald Trump , who has close ties to Huang and called him a “very high quality person” after the scandal broke, insisted he had no idea that U.S. intelligence found Huang’s mistress, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. But the New York Times reported in late October that Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago and chose not to take action.
Earlier Tuesday, Huang released his first public statement since leaving Nvidia, admitting that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote on X.
Huang acknowledged the push from supporters to reinstate him as Nvidia’s CEO and said he’d be “honored to answer these calls.”
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.
“NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.
But, as Nvidia’s board said during the earnings call later Tuesday, that won’t be in the cards — for now.

articles.title_orig: A string of tech outages disrupted flights, banking, and major apps. Here's what officials have said about the causes.
articles.title_zh: A string of tech outages disrupted flights, banking, and major apps. Here's what officials have said about the causes.
articles.content_orig:
If you feel like the digital world is ending , you're not alone.
A string of high-profile technology outages over the past week has disrupted the lives of many Americans trying to travel, transfer money, or make purchases, and caused speculation that something bigger and more nefarious could be going on.
There has been no indication from government officials or the companies affected that cyberattacks or AI were responsible. And despite the uncanny timing, there are no signs the incidents were connected.
"At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort," Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence committee, said in a statement Tuesday, adding that the evidence suggested the outages were due to "legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity."
Warner said AI was allowing vulnerabilities to be identified faster and creating pressure to fix them immediately, "putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change."
"These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call," he said. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences."
Here are the major outages reported and what we know about each one.
Microsoft experienced a major outage last week that impacted its 365 tool suite, affecting products such as Outlook, Teams, and Copilot.
By late Friday morning, the company said services were stabilizing.
Microsoft said the cause of the outage was "technical" and "not related to cyber or AI / agents."
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday, citing issues with its air traffic control systems.
Flights were grounded for over four hours, leading to thousands of delays and cancellations on Friday and Saturday.
Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed the outage on aging air traffic control infrastructure.
Mullin said they did not believe the outage was related to cybersecurity or an AI attack.
JPMorgan Chase said Monday said it experienced service issues related to a "software bug in on-premise hardware systems."
Customers had reported issues accessing account information and delayed transactions. Customers of other banks also reported issues, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and US Bank, with the latter saying customers attempting to use Chase's Zelle may have been affected.
"There is no evidence this is cyber-related," Chase said.
United Airlines on Monday said it fixed a "technology issue" after a system outage caused delays to departing flights.
The airline said flights in progress and United Express flights weren't affected. United had 945 delayed flights on Monday, according to the flight tracking site FlightAware.
"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," United said.
Charles Schwab experienced issues with its website on Tuesday. Some users were unable to access the site, which temporarily displayed a message that said its server "encountered an internal error or misconfiguration and was unable to complete your request."
The spokesperson for the brokerage firm said a "brief webpage loading issue has been resolved."
Apple said an "internal update" caused outages to some of its services after users online said they were having issues accessing Apple Pay and iCloud.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," Apple said in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."
Apple said the incident was not a cyberattack.

articles.title_orig: Student accused of taking photos of planes for Chinese Communist Party to be detained pending trial
articles.title_zh: Student accused of taking photos of planes for Chinese Communist Party to be detained pending trial
articles.content_orig:
A college student accused of working with a Chinese Communist Party representative to take photos of American airplanes and logistic hubs in Chicago — and lying about it to U.S. investigators — will be detained pending trial, a federal judge ruled Tuesday.
Detroit-based federal Magistrate Judge Kimberly Altman denied a request from lawyers for Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese citizen who is currently an undergraduate at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, to remain free and return to Canada as his case proceeds.
According to the Justice Department, Zeng's legal team said in a court hearing Tuesday that his family would "pay any bond amount this court could impose" to keep their client out of detention, and suggested the family could even buy an apartment in the United States for Zeng to be bonded to.
Zeng was indicted earlier this month on one count of making false statements to a government agency. Prosecutors allege he sneaked into a FedEx property at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport and took photos of the facility, then later lied about the purpose of his trip to the United States to customs officials, calling it "hobby photography."
Zeng pleaded not guilty earlier this month . He hasn't explicitly been charged with taking photos of planes, but instead was charged with lying to investigators.
A criminal complaint filed in the Eastern District of Michigan alleges that in April, Zeng took photographs of the FedEx facility, climbed on a parked forklift and attempted to open locked trailers. The Justice Department says surveillance footage shows Zeng attempting to open a shipping container and using the forklift to take photos at a higher vantage point.
After leaving the country, Zeng attempted to reenter the U.S. on Aug. 23 through Detroit's Ambassador Bridge, which links Canada and Michigan, and was flagged for additional screening based on the April incident. He was then interviewed three subsequent times by Customs and Border Protection agents.
In his third interview, Zeng stated that a Chinese contact assigned him specific planes and tail numbers to photograph and that he would be paid between $20 and $30 per photo, according to the criminal complaint. Zeng said that he talked to the contact using SIM cards that were sent to him by mail, and after talking, he would destroy the SIM cards, delete the conversations and delete the photos that he had taken.
He allegedly told customs officers that the contact approached him on an "aviation spotter website" and said he believed the person was connected to the Chinese Communist Party, and was told that the photos were going to be used for "research."
Zeng was then interviewed by the FBI, the complaint says. He allegedly told law enforcement the contact was interested in getting photographs of rare airplanes, and believed the contact worked for the Chinese government because "when he started making more requests, the language he used was very organized and managed, not language typically used between friends." The photos, Zeng said, were also of "American United" aircraft at O'Hare.
Federal investigators said it was only after further questioning from the FBI that Zeng admitted that he had messaged with the contact for three months and said he wanted to help the contact because "he thought it was 'cool' and wanted 'to have the opportunity to work with someone like [agents] at the FBI.'"
He told the FBI that the contact wanted him to find out more about transportation and logistics in the United States, and wanted him to travel to Orlando, Las Vegas and Los Angeles to "obtain photographs of specific locations surrounding airports."
Zeng said he denied those tasks.
His lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the detention order.

articles.title_orig: Sean Duffy’s $50 billion demand for air travel fixes is met with yelling and skepticism in Congress
articles.title_zh: Sean Duffy’s $50 billion demand for air travel fixes is met with yelling and skepticism in Congress
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s request for $50.1 billion in new Federal Aviation Administration funding after a nationwide ground stop strangled air travel is running into skepticism from both parties on Capitol Hill.
The funding request was suddenly increased from $30 billion after the hourslong ground stop Friday caused delays and cancellations for passengers across thousands of flights.
The formal funding ask was conveyed in a Tuesday letter signed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the failure, blaming it on predecessors and Congress. The letter, cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.”
After publicly reproaching Congress for the failure last week, Duffy met privately with Senate Republicans on Tuesday to make his case on Capitol Hill.
The closed-door briefing was contentious. The transportation secretary was “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators during his briefing, according to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion.
When it was over, Senate Republican leaders and Duffy notably held their news conferences separately.
Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., stopped short of endorsing the full funding figure, saying only that the GOP is unified around the belief that “safe skies is an incredibly important priority.”
“We will see what the traffic will bear, what’s achievable,” he said, calling it a “discussion to be had” on the dollar amount.
Duffy met with only Republicans on Tuesday, not Democrats — even though the regular government funding process requires bipartisan support.
And Democrats were left wanting a better explanation, particularly as Duffy has pointed fingers at them. And members in both parties noted that President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up.
“Look, we have not been given the answers. They have not come clean,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told reporters on Tuesday. “At his first press conference, all Duffy did was attack Democrats, and he asked for $50 billion when they haven’t even spent the $12 billion we’ve given to them. I have little faith in them.”
Facing Republican questions on the matter, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation.
Other Democrats are vexed by the FAA funding request.
“I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
The issue is wrapped up in a larger debate about funding the government ahead of a Dec. 11 deadline to avoid another shutdown . Congress could either reach a deal by then on new funding, punt it to next year with a stopgap bill, or fail to act and allow a shutdown.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said air traffic control is “absolutely not a partisan issue” and that Congress will work to make sure that any funding is “paid for in a responsible way.”
Republicans are also considering a party-line “reconciliation” bill to approve military funding without the need for Democratic votes; Democrats are likely to resist additional military funds unless the Iran war comes to an end. Other provisions could be added to such a bill — if it materializes before Republicans lose control of Congress. Thune indicated Tuesday that it is still an open question, as Republicans would need to pass a budget resolution by Thanksgiving to pull it off. It would be a long, arduous process requiring near-total GOP unity in both chambers, and it would need to begin soon in order to finish this year.
Duffy said he’s agnostic on how the funds get passed when asked by NBC News why he only met with Republicans on Tuesday.
“I have met with Democrats. I’ve spent hours on the phone with Democrats. Get along with them well. They understand this issue,” Duffy said Tuesday, speaking to reporters separately after meeting with GOP senators. “I’m not going to tell them how to do their work, but I’m telling everybody what we need. I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them work their process.”
One of the Democrats whom Duffy spoke to was House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely next House speaker.
“I appreciated the conversation,” Jeffries told reporters. “There are still more questions than answers in terms of what happened, why it happened, how do we prevent it from happening again.”
Jeffries added that he wants a briefing on the FAA ground stop and other recent outages, saying: “These developments are troubling, and it’s unclear if it’s all infrastructure-related or whether there’s some malignant activity.”
When asked about Duffy’s $50.1 billion request, outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said Republicans would work with the administration to fund “as much of that as we can.” He pointed to the $12.5 billion already approved for FAA modernization and did not specify a timeline or whether Congress would pursue a supplemental funding package.
I am a field producer for NBC News based in Washington, D.C., covering all things politics.

Talk about a pressure test!

Former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has said he would be “honoured” to return to the company after he was ousted in the wake of a scandal.
Mr Huang resigned from the chipmaker last week, amid a wave of scandal after he admitted to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy as well as a subordinate at Nvidia . Since then, petitions and supporters have called for him to return – but the company has said that it is not interested in inviting him back.
Nonetheless, Mr Huang signalled he would be willing to return and that he would work with an investigation into the incident. But he suggested that the decision was up to the board and whether it thought his return would be “in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America”.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in his first public statement since he resigned on 12 November over revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the chip firm's China business. Mr Huang had not been quoted in Nvidia’s original statement about his departure, though it thanked him for his “profound” contributions to the company, and he has been silent since.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he said in the new statement.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Mr Huang's statement, but multiple reports have suggested that its board is not planning to reappoint him. Nvidia shares ⁠pared some declines and were last down 1 per cent.
More than 180,000 people have signed a petition demanding Huang’s return, Elon Musk has thrown his support behind the effort, ⁠and US President Donald Trump said he would not mind seeing Huang reinstated as CEO. Thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees have joined the call, even as governance experts and some investors warn that bringing him back before investigations are complete could expose the company to fresh risks.
The groundswell of support for Huang has turned a corporate succession story into a test of whether Nvidia can separate itself from a founder whose influence stretches across its employees — some fiercely loyal to the former CEO — and shareholders, Silicon Valley, the Taiwanese supply chain and Washington.
Taiwan's tallest skyscraper, Taipei 101, was illuminated on Monday with messages including "Taiwan Loves Jensen." Some prominent shareholders such as Atreides ⁠Management's Gavin Baker and Altimeter Capital Management CEO Brad Gerstner have urged Nvidia not to rush to replace him ​before ⁠all the facts are known.
Earlier on Tuesday, before Mr Huang’s statement, Nvidia created a board-level ​committee ⁠to oversee national security and export controls, its first major governance move since he left.
Mr Huang's relationships have raised questions about whether Nvidia's oversight kept pace with its rapid growth and increasing importance to US national security. The crisis had erased more ⁠than $400 billion from the company's market value by Monday's close.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, ​a former Goldman Sachs ⁠vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of ‌law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
In the full statement, posted on X, Mr Huang thanked the public for its support and admitted to having made “serious mistakes”. He also included a message to his family, in which he suggested they were offering him “support”.
“Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me,” he wrote.
“I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO.
“Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.”
